articles.title: Who Decides an Artist Matters?
articles.summary: Museums, prizes and the odd auction room moment. A look at how eleven artists we follow came to be taken seriously, and what that recognition leaves out.
articles.description: A reported essay on how artists gain standing through museum shows, prizes and biennials, from Richter and Kusama at Tate Modern to OSGEMEOS, KAWS, Vhils, Eko Nugroho and Faith XLVII.
articles.body:
Ask how an artist becomes important and you get two kinds of answer. One is about the work: what it looks like, how it is made, what it changed. The other is about people: the curators, juries and crowds who decide, over years, which work is worth looking at again. This is a reported essay about the second kind, drawn from museum, prize and press records listed below.

The museum invitation

For many artists the clearest sign of standing is a large museum show. Tate Modern has given several of the artists we write about that moment. Gerhard Richter's retrospective, Panorama, opened there in October 2011, and Tate's announcement described him as widely regarded as one of the most important artists working today. Yayoi Kusama's Infinity Mirror Rooms opened at Tate Modern in May 2021 and stayed until April 2024, close to three years.

El Anatsui was given the Turbine Hall. His Hyundai Commission, Behind the Red Moon, opened on 9 October 2023, and Tate called it the largest work he had made.

Timing can say as much as the invitation. S.H. Raza had worked in France for decades before the Centre Pompidou gave him a retrospective in 2023, seven years after his death. The Art Newspaper described it as his first show in a state-run museum. Beatriz Milhazes had been showing internationally since the 1990s when the Guggenheim gave her the first New York museum show devoted to her work, in 2025.

Prizes for a whole career

Some honours are given for a single show. Others are given for a life's work. The Praemium Imperiale, awarded in Japan, went to Richter for painting in 1997 and to Kusama in 2006. El Anatsui received the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the Venice Biennale in 2015, and the Praemium Imperiale two years later.

National honours count too, though they are read differently abroad. Raza received India's Padma Shri in 1981, the Padma Bhushan in 2007 and the Padma Vibhushan in 2013. France made him a Commandeur of the Légion d'honneur in 2015.

Artists who started outside

For artists who began on the street, the route in looks different. In 2008 Tate Modern invited six artists, among them the twin brothers known as OSGEMEOS, to paint its river front. Tate called the show the first major public museum display of street art in London.

Others followed in their own cities and their own time. The Brooklyn Museum gave KAWS a survey of more than 100 works in 2021, from early graffiti drawings to large sculpture. In Lisbon, MAAT showed Vhils' video installation Prisma in 2022, and MUDE, the city's design museum, showed his printed editions in early 2026. Eko Nugroho was one of five artists in Indonesia's pavilion at the Venice Biennale in 2013. In 2025 the STRAAT Museum in Amsterdam showed Faith XLVII with her son and another artist, and added one of her works to its collection.

And then there is Banksy

Banksy is the clearest case of an artist whose standing was built almost entirely outside these systems. His best known moment came in an auction room. In 2018 a Girl with Balloon shredded itself just after the hammer fell at Sotheby's. Three years later the renamed Love Is in the Bin was sold again at Sotheby's London, and The Art Newspaper reported a price of £18.6m with fees.

What recognition does and does not tell you

A museum show, a prize or a place in a pavilion is a judgement made by particular people at a particular time. It makes the work easier to see and easier to take seriously. It does not settle whether the work is good, and it does not tell you whether you will like it.

It also misses a great deal. Many artists are better known in their own region than in London or New York, and many of the walls these artists painted were never reviewed by anyone. The record above is a starting point for looking, not a ranking.

articles.title: OSGEMEOS, Two Brothers and One World
articles.summary: Twin brothers from São Paulo who started on the walls and never stopped painting the same imagined place.
articles.description: A reported profile of OSGEMEOS: graffiti in São Paulo, a painted Scottish castle and the dream world they carry from walls to canvas.
articles.alt: Two men in caps stand on a New York pavement, one with arms folded and the other looking down at a music player, both in clothes spattered with paint.
articles.credit: Otávio and Gustavo Pandolfo, the twins who work as OSGEMEOS, in New York in April 2007. Photo: Fatima Haidara, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
articles.body:
OSGEMEOS is a name for two people. Gustavo and Otavio Pandolfo are twin brothers, born in 1974, and the name means “the twins” in Portuguese. This is a reported essay, drawn from the records listed below.

From the street

They started as graffiti artists in São Paulo. Artsy, which tracks their career, lists the influences as Brazilian folk culture, hip-hop and the graffiti scene that first gave them walls to paint.

A castle in Scotland

In May 2007 the London street art blog Hookedblog reported a month-long project at Kelburn Castle in Ayrshire. OSGEMEOS, Nina Pandolfo and Nunca came from Brazil to paint the castle's walls and turrets alongside Scottish artists, living in the castle while they worked. Four years later Hyperallergic reported that the owners wanted the paint to stay.

The same world, indoors

Their figures are thin and yellow-skinned, dressed in patterned clothes. Indoors the brothers add things a wall cannot hold. One 2010 panel at Christie's combined acrylic, spray enamel, latex and sequins. A 2005 work sold by Phillips came with its own audio player and headphones.

What is not known

How the two divide the work is not recorded in the sources we read. They sign as one, and we have reported them as one.

articles.title: Vhils and the Portrait in the Wall
articles.summary: A Lisbon artist who makes faces by taking the city apart, one layer at a time.
articles.description: A reported profile of Vhils, Alexandre Farto: Lisbon graffiti, art school in London and a method built on removal.
articles.alt: Vhils, a dark-haired, bearded man in a black T-shirt and dark trousers, standing by a wall of chipped pale plaster with a hammer in his hand, seen from above.
articles.credit: Vhils at work in Beja, Portugal, in 2017. Photo: Nicola Di Nunzio, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
articles.body:
Most artists add paint. Alexandre Farto, who works as Vhils, takes it away. This is a reported essay. Much of what is known about his career comes from his own website, and we say so where it does.

Lisbon

Farto was born in Lisbon in 1987. His site says he began working on the city's walls as Vhils in the early 2000s, at a time when Lisbon was changing quickly, and that he went on to study in London at Byam Shaw School of Art and Central Saint Martins.

Scratching the surface

His site calls the method subtraction. He cuts, drills, etches or blasts through a surface until a face appears. The first walls made this way were shown in Lisbon in 2007, and at the Cans Festival in London in 2008, which the site names as the moment his work became known abroad.

The same idea in the studio

The studio pieces use the street as material. Attrition series #01, sold at Bonhams in 2025, is a stack of advertising posters collected from the street and carved by hand. The colours of old adverts become the shadows of a face.

What is not known

The site reports work in more than 30 countries. We have not found an independent list to check that against.

articles.title: KAWS and the Cartoon That Grew Up
articles.summary: From bus shelter adverts to a balloon over Manhattan: how Brian Donnelly built a career around one crossed-out face.
articles.description: A reported profile of KAWS, Brian Donnelly: graffiti, animation work, the COMPANION toy and the move from street to sculpture.
articles.body:
KAWS is the name Brian Donnelly, born in 1974, chose to write on walls. According to Christie's, he chose it because he liked how the four letters looked together. This is a reported essay, drawn from the records listed below.

Walls, then adverts

Donnelly studied illustration at the School of Visual Arts in New York and painted backgrounds for television cartoons. He tagged buildings in New Jersey and Manhattan, then moved to bus shelters, painting his own cartoon figures into the adverts behind the glass.

A toy with crossed-out eyes

In 1999, on a visit to Japan with the brand Bounty Hunter, he made his first toy, COMPANION. Christie's reports that the edition of 500 sold out almost at once. The figure, with X's for eyes, became the centre of his work.

Bigger and bigger

In 2012 a COMPANION balloon floated through Manhattan in the Macy's Thanksgiving parade. In 2019 a 37 metre inflatable lay in Hong Kong's Victoria Harbour. In the studio, a 2011 fibreglass COMPANION stands almost two and a half metres tall.

Where he sits

Christie's notes that critics compare him with Basquiat and Haring, who also came from the street, and with Warhol and Koons. He names Takashi Murakami's collaborations as an influence. Whether a cartoon on this scale is still a joke is a question his work keeps open.

articles.title: Eko Nugroho, Masks and Thread
articles.summary: A Yogyakarta artist whose masked comic figures turn up on walls, in embroidery and in a national museum.
articles.description: A reported profile of Eko Nugroho: Yogyakarta, community projects, masked figures and the move from paint to thread.
articles.body:
Eko Nugroho was born in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, in 1977, and still lives and works there. This is a reported essay, drawn from the museum and auction house records listed below.

Working with others

The Singapore Art Museum describes him as an artist who often works with communities and other creatives to draw attention to social issues. He works in painting, embroidery and sculpture, and Phillips has sold his work in batik on cotton.

Why the masks

His figures come from comics and almost always wear masks. The museum gives a reason: he avoids stereotyped faces that could lead to discriminatory readings of his work.

From wall to thread

In Illusion (2007), now in the Singapore Art Museum, a masked figure stands in a stripped landscape full of monster-like machines. The museum reads it as a picture of environmental “crispy crisis”. It is made in embroidery, and it keeps the flat, bold look of a drawing on a wall.

On the map

He showed at the 5th Asia Pacific Triennial in Brisbane in 2006, and later at the Singapore Art Museum and National Gallery Singapore.

articles.title: Faith XLVII, From Faith47 to 39 Countries
articles.summary: A South African graffiti writer who took her quiet figures from local walls to murals around the world.
articles.description: A reported profile of Faith XLVII: graffiti in South Africa from 1997, murals in 39 countries and a practice that grew beyond the wall.
articles.alt: A tall painted figure in a dark hooded robe, face lifted and lit from one side, fills the pale green end wall of a block of flats. Bare trees stand in front and ivy climbs the brick beside it.
articles.credit: Mural by Faith XLVII on the end wall of a block of flats in Cologne, photographed in February 2015. Photo: Raimond Spekking, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
articles.body:
Faith XLVII was born in 1979 and began writing graffiti on South African streets in 1997, under the name Faith47. This is a reported essay, drawn from the auction house records listed below.

Leaving home

In 2006, according to Strauss & Co, she began travelling to paint public murals. The count now stands at 39 countries. One of them is Capax Infiniti, painted in 2014 on the side of the Carlyle building in Portland, Oregon. The Latin means “holding the infinite”.

Beyond the wall

Her work has grown into new media installations, hand-sewn wall hangings, bronzes, paintings and prints. Wall images come back as prints: the Portland mural later became a lithograph with the same name.

Three words

One triptych, sold by Strauss & Co in June 2024, is called Coltan; Oil; Diamonds. Three resources mined in Africa, each on a tall panel in a frame she made by hand. It joins the quiet, almost religious mood of her figures to a hard subject.

Where it is seen

Strauss lists her work in collections including Universal Studios in Los Angeles and the Cyril Ramaphosa Foundation, and shows at the Brooklyn Museum and the Bernard Magrez Foundation in France.

articles.title: Yayoi Kusama, One Mark Over and Over
articles.summary: The Japanese artist who died in August 2026 spent seven decades repeating a single mark until it filled canvases, objects and rooms.
articles.description: A reported profile of Yayoi Kusama: Kyoto training, the New York Infinity Nets, the dots and mirror rooms, and the record set at Sotheby's in November 2026.
articles.alt: Close view of Yayoi Kusama's face, with dark hair, red lipstick and pale pink glasses in a decorative silver frame.
articles.credit: Yayoi Kusama, around 2004. A still from George Quasha's film series art is (Speaking Portraits). Photo: George Quasha, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
articles.body:
Yayoi Kusama died in a Tokyo hospital on 14 August 2026, aged 97. Her foundation announced the death on 27 August. Three months later one of her earliest paintings set a new auction record for her work. The gap between those two facts says something about how long the paintings took to be understood.

Kyoto, then New York

She was born in Matsumoto in 1929 and studied Japanese-style painting in Kyoto in 1948. In 1957 she left for the United States, and by 1958 she was in New York, where she stayed until 1973.

The Net

The New York paintings are the Infinity Nets: canvases covered edge to edge in small looped brushmarks. There is no centre and no border to the pattern. It stops only where the canvas stops. One of them, No. 3P.B. of 1960, was shown in the Whitney Museum's annual exhibition in 1961. On 16 November 2026 it sold at Sotheby's New York for about US$15 million with fees, according to The Art Newspaper.

From net to dot to room

The same repeated mark later became the dot, carried onto pumpkins, sculptures and whole rooms. In the mirror rooms the repetition has no end at all. She first showed at the Venice Biennale in 1966, with Narcissus Garden, and represented Japan there in 1993.

What is not settled

Reports of the November sale disagree on which earlier record it replaced. Artsy names a 2022 sale at Phillips; HENI News names a 2023 sale in Hong Kong. We have not tried to settle it.

articles.title: Beatriz Milhazes, Painting Without a Brush
articles.summary: The Rio painter paints on plastic and presses the paint onto canvas, building pictures out of flowers, circles and Carnival colour.
articles.description: A reported profile of Beatriz Milhazes: the 1980s Generation, the plastic-sheet method, and the Brazilian sources behind her patterns.
articles.body:
Beatriz Milhazes paints her pictures twice. First on a sheet of plastic, then, once the paint has dried, by pressing that sheet face down onto the canvas and peeling it away. What stays behind is flat, with no brushstrokes, and carries small tears and wrinkles from the transfer.

Rio de Janeiro

She was born in Rio de Janeiro in 1960 and works there. She is associated with the 1980s Generation of Brazilian painters. She showed at the Carnegie International in 1995, in Brazil's pavilion at the Venice Biennale in 2003, and had her first survey in the United States at the Pérez Art Museum Miami in 2015.

What goes into the pattern

Phillips' catalogue for Paraty (2001 to 2002) lists her sources: Baroque architecture, lace, Carnival decoration and the plants of Rio's botanical garden. The painting takes its name from the coastal town where her mother was born. The same catalogue links her to the Brazilian modernist idea of taking in outside influences and making them local.

How to look

Find the geometry first, the bands and circles, then watch the flowers slide over and under them. The pictures are crowded on purpose.

articles.title: S.H. Raza, From the Village to the Dot
articles.summary: An Indian painter who spent sixty years in France moved from landscapes of Provence and Corsica to the bindu, a single black dot.
articles.description: A reported profile of S.H. Raza: the Progressive Artists' Group, Paris, the French landscapes and the Bindu paintings from 1980.
articles.alt: S.H. Raza, an elderly man with white hair and glasses in a pale suit, seated and leaning over a sheet of paper as people gather close around him.
articles.credit: S.H. Raza at an art summit in Delhi, January 2011. Photo: Chetan Nikam, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
articles.body:
S.H. Raza's paintings begin with villages and end with a dot. The distance between the two took him most of a working life, much of it spent far from India.

Bombay

He was born in 1922 in Kakkaiya, in what is now Madhya Pradesh, and trained in Nagpur and at the Sir J. J. School of Art in Bombay. In 1947 he was one of the founders of the Progressive Artists' Group there.

France

In 1950 he went to Paris on a French government scholarship and studied at the École des Beaux-Arts. In 1956 he became the first artist from outside France to win the Prix de la Critique. His French landscapes are built of blocks of thick paint: Village Otta Corse (1958), a village in Corsica, is one. By the 1960s the forms loosen into large dark fields, as in La Provence Noire (1965).

The bindu

From 1980 the bindu, a black dot, sits at the centre of his work, with circles, triangles and bands of colour around it. He moved back to India late in life (Wikipedia gives both 2010 and 2011) and died in New Delhi in July 2016.

articles.title: Gerhard Richter, the Blur and the Squeegee
articles.summary: The German painter has worked in two strands at once: photographs copied and blurred, and abstracts left partly to chance.
articles.description: A reported profile of Gerhard Richter: Dresden, the move west in 1961, Capitalist Realism, the photo paintings and the squeegee abstracts.
articles.alt: Portrait of Gerhard Richter, an older man with white hair, a short white beard and round dark glasses, in a dark coat, looking at the camera.
articles.credit: Gerhard Richter at the National Gallery, Prague, in April 2017. Photo: Jindřich Nosek (NoJin), CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
articles.body:
Gerhard Richter has never settled on one way to paint. For most of his career he has worked in two strands side by side, and each seems to argue with the other.

East to West

He was born in Dresden in 1932 and studied at the Dresden Academy of Fine Arts from 1951. In 1961, two months before the Berlin Wall went up, he left for West Germany and continued his studies in Düsseldorf. With Sigmar Polke and Konrad Lueg he took up the label Capitalist Realism. He has lived in Cologne since 1983.

The blur

The first strand starts with a photograph, copied onto canvas and softened with a dry brush. Kerze (Candle) of 1982 is one: a single candle, painted from a photograph and blurred. The Art Newspaper reports that it sold at Christie's New York in May 2026 from the collection of the dealer Marian Goodman.

The squeegee

The second strand, from the mid-1980s, is abstract. Layers of paint are dragged across the canvas with a large squeegee, so that colours scrape, tear and show through. Abstraktes Bild of 1991, two metres tall, is a large example. The artist sets the conditions; the paint decides the details.

articles.title: Banksy, the Artist Who Isn't There
articles.summary: No confirmed name, no public face. How an anonymous artist from Bristol built a body of work, and a way of proving it is his.
articles.description: A reported profile of Banksy: the Bristol beginnings, the early move to canvas, Pest Control and the joke as a method, drawn from museum and auction house records.
articles.alt: A dark statue seen from below against a grey sky: a man in a suit strides off the edge of a stone plinth while a large flag he holds blows back over his face, with scaffolded buildings behind.
articles.credit: Statue by Banksy in Waterloo Place, London, installed in April 2026. Photographed in May 2026. Photo: Bex Walton, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
articles.body:
Banksy has never publicly said who he is. For an artist whose canvases now sell for millions, that is an unusual position, and it shapes how everything else about him is known. This is a reported essay: it draws on museum and auction house records, listed below, not on any meeting with the artist.

Bristol first

The record begins in Bristol. A research guide from the Jordan Schnitzer Museum of Art places him as a teenage graffiti writer there in the 1990s, before a move to London. Phillips, in its catalogue, dates the first works on trains and walls to 1993.

The stencil came early. It is quick to use and the image it leaves reads at once, which suits work made in public, at speed, by someone who would rather not be seen making it.

From the wall to the canvas

The move indoors happened sooner than many assume. Laugh Now, a canvas of a chimpanzee wearing a sandwich board that says one day they will be in charge, was painted in 2001 and bought from the artist that same year, according to Bonhams. A year later the same image ran six metres long on a wall commissioned by the Ocean Rooms nightclub in Brighton.

By 2006 he was showing large canvases in a warehouse exhibition in Los Angeles called Barely Legal. Angel, a black and white figure against a dark field more than two metres square, was among them, and was bought by its owner directly from the artist.

A name that certifies

An anonymous artist still needs a way to say what is his. Banksy's answer is Pest Control, his own authentication body. Every recent auction lot we checked, from Laugh Now to a small cut-out canvas of a rat reaching for a red heart, came with its certificate.

That arrangement turns the absent artist into a kind of signature. The work is known to be his because his office says so, not because anyone has watched him make it.

The joke as a method

Rats, chimpanzees and children recur because they let him point at people without drawing them. Bonhams' catalogue calls the chimpanzee a stand-in through which human hierarchies can be seen. The humour comes first, and the point a second later.

The best-known joke was played on the art market itself. In October 2018 a framed Girl with Balloon was partly shredded by a device in its frame moments after it sold at Sotheby's London. The work was renamed Love Is in the Bin.

What is not known

Quite a lot. Auction houses do not even agree on his year of birth: Bonhams catalogues him as born in 1974 on one lot and 1975 on another. We have not tried to settle that, or the question of who he is. The work, at least, is on the record.

articles.title: When an Artist Is Also a Celebrity
articles.summary: A famous name gets the work seen. It also means most people have made up their minds before they look.
articles.description: Fame opens gallery doors and closes minds. An essay on celebrity artists, from Warhol to Amanza Smith, and how to look at their work fairly.
articles.body:
There are two kinds of famous artist. One becomes well known because of the art. The other is well known already and then begins to show art. The art world tends to admire the first and distrust the second.

Fame made by art

Andy Warhol is the model for the first kind. He treated fame as a material. He painted film stars, ran a studio that was also a social scene, founded a magazine and turned himself into one of the most recognisable figures of his century.

Britain had its own version in the 1990s. Damien Hirst put a shark in a tank. Tracey Emin showed her own unmade bed. Both became household names, known to people who had never been inside a gallery.

In these cases the celebrity grew out of the work, and nobody now doubts that they were artists first.

Fame that arrives first

The second kind has a harder time. Amanza Smith was known to television audiences from the series Selling Sunset before she showed a painting. When she made her debut at MASH Gallery in Los Angeles, the gallery described her as multifaceted and no stranger to reinvention.

Her canvases are large, layered and full of colour, with collage, graffiti-like marks and, in recent work, robotic forms. In April 2025 they were shown in Palma at the opening of a Grove Gallery space, beside work by Zara Muse and Silent Mike.

The suspicion such artists meet is easy to understand. Galleries want visitors, and a famous name brings them. So people wonder whether the work would be on the wall without it.

The opposite choice

It is striking how many artists run the other way. Konn Artiss is anonymous. Zen Xander's own website says the anonymity is there to keep the focus on the work and away from fame. These artists have looked at fame and decided it would get in the way.

So the same art world holds people who are known and want to be judged as artists, and artists who refuse to be known at all.

Looking fairly

How should a viewer handle this? Not by pretending the name is absent. You cannot unknow who made a picture.

But you can notice what the name is doing to your judgement. If you would walk past the work with an unknown signature, fame is flattering it. If you would stop for it and are dismissing it because of who made it, fame is costing it. Both are errors.

The fair test is the dull one. Give it the time you would give anything else. Look at the colour, the surface, the decisions. Then ask whether you would want to see it again.

A longer view

Time settles most of these questions. Celebrity fades faster than paint. In fifty years few people will remember who was on which television programme, and the pictures will have to manage alone. That is the real test, and it applies to everyone.

articles.title: Why Collectors Buy Faces
articles.summary: A landscape gives you somewhere to look. A portrait looks back. That may be the whole explanation.
articles.description: Portraits are among the most sought-after works in contemporary art. An essay on why people want to live with a painted face.
articles.body:
Ask people what art they would hang at home and many will say a view: sea, hills, a street they love. Yet some of the most talked-about sales in contemporary art are of faces. It is worth asking why.

The oldest subject

For most of history a portrait was bought by the person in it. It recorded rank, marked a marriage or kept a likeness after death. The buyer and the subject were the same household.

Today that link has almost gone. Collectors buy portraits of strangers, of public figures, of people the artist knows and they never will.

What the market shows

The prices suggest the appetite is real. Art Plugged reported that Zara Muse's portrait of Malala Yousafzai sold at Bonhams in London in April 2025 for £51,200 including premium. Ocula records that Amoako Boafo's The Lemon Bathing Suit made £675,000 at auction in 2020, a year after it was painted.

Museums tell the same story. In 2018 the National Portrait Gallery in London showed Njideka Akunyili Crosby's series The Beautyful Ones. In 2024 the Belvedere in Vienna gave Boafo more than fifty works' worth of wall.

A caution is due. A handful of results is not a study of the market, and we do not claim that portraits outsell everything else. These are examples of demand, nothing more.

Three reasons

Why would someone want a stranger's face in the sitting room? We can suggest three reasons.

The first is company. A room with a portrait in it has someone else in it. People who live with one often talk about it as a presence.

The second is values. To hang a portrait of Malala Yousafzai is to say something about what you admire. Muse has said she chose the subject for bravery and strength. The buyer is choosing those too.

The third is recognition. For a long time the faces on gallery walls were drawn from a narrow slice of the world. Boafo turned to portraits of Black sitters after moving to Vienna, where by several accounts he found them largely missing from what was shown. For many collectors, buying such a portrait is a way of putting right what was missing.

The hand in the face

There is a fourth reason, which has to do with how these pictures are made. Muse builds faces with a knife. Boafo paints skin with his fingers. Akunyili Crosby fills hers with transferred photographs.

In each case the making is visible in the face itself. In a time when any image can be produced in seconds, a face that clearly took a person days to make has a pull of its own.

Looking back

The simplest answer may still be the best. We are built to look at faces. We read them before we can read anything else. A painted face, hung where you pass it every day, never quite becomes furniture.

articles.title: The Artist's Name as a Brand
articles.summary: Zara Muse, Zen Xander, Konn Artiss, Vhils, JR, Mr Dot. Count how many of the artists in these pages work under a name they chose.
articles.description: Working names, pseudonyms and collectives: how contemporary artists use a name as a shield, a signature and a brand.
articles.body:
Artists have always signed their work. What is newer is how many now sign it with a name that is not on their passport.

A name as a shield

Some choose a working name for privacy. Zara Muse is the professional name of Alexandra Johnson, who has said it gives her a degree of separation between her life and her work. The paintings can travel to hotels, auctions and other countries. The person can stay at home.

Others go further and withhold the person altogether. Konn Artiss is anonymous. JR is a pseudonym, and his full identity has never been officially confirmed. In both cases the secrecy has a practical side, since much of the work is done in public without asking.

A name as a tag

For artists who began in graffiti, the chosen name comes first. Vhils is the tag Alexandre Farto used as a teenage graffiti writer around Lisbon. A tag is a signature designed to be written fast and recognised at a distance. That is also a fair description of a logo.

A name as a group

A name does not have to belong to one person. Zen Xander has been described in the press as an anonymous street artist. The artist's own website says it is a small collective of painters, illustrators, designers and writers working toward a shared style.

That is less strange than it sounds. The workshops of the old masters turned out paintings under one name with many hands involved. El Anatsui's vast hangings are assembled by teams. The single signature has often stood for a studio.

A name as a character

Then there are names that work as characters. Clarke Reynolds, who makes art from braille, also appears as Mr Dot, a figure he uses to reach children. The name does a job the artist's own could not.

When the name becomes the product

Once a name is recognised, it can be attached to things. Limited edition prints, signed and numbered, are the simplest case. Hotel residencies are another. Fashion is a third: in 2020 Amoako Boafo worked with Dior on a menswear collection that carried the textures of his portraits onto clothes.

None of this is new. Andy Warhol understood sixty years ago that an artist's name could work like a company's. What has changed is the speed. A name can now go from a wall to a product in a couple of years.

What to make of it

It is tempting to be cynical. A chosen name can look like marketing, and sometimes it is.

But there is another way to see it. A working name lets the art be judged a little more on its own. It protects people who would not otherwise show their work. It lets several people speak with one voice. The name on the label is a decision, like every other decision in the picture, and it is worth asking what it is doing there.

articles.title: From Gallery Wall to Hotel Wall: The Gallery in Residence
articles.summary: A hotel used to buy its art once and hang it for twenty years. Now some are borrowing a gallery instead.
articles.description: Galleries are placing changing displays of art in hotels. A feature on the gallery in residence model, with Silent Mike at Dorsett Shepherds Bush as a case study.
articles.body:
Walk into most hotels and the art is part of the fit-out, chosen with the carpet and expected to last as long. A different arrangement has been spreading. A gallery takes over the walls, hangs a show, and a few months later hangs another.

How it works

The idea is borrowed from the artist residency, where a maker is given a place to work for a set time. Here it is the gallery, or one of its artists, that takes up residence. The hotel gets a changing display it did not have to buy. The gallery gets a second set of walls and a new audience walking past them.

A west London example

In March 2025 the Dorsett hotel in Shepherds Bush announced a partnership with Grove Gallery and named its first artist in residence: Silent Mike.

Art Plugged reported that the show, Chromatic Shift, placed fifteen works through the hotel's main bar and restaurant and opened to the public on 28 March. It was a change of direction for the artist. His 2023 debut at Quantus Gallery in London, Introspective, had been entirely in black and white. The new pieces were in full colour.

The method is worth describing. According to the same report, each piece is built from machine-cut wooden circles with hand-sanded surfaces, finished in layers of paint, primer and a glossy paste. The hotel described intricate geometric patterns combined with elements of classical sculpture, and Art Plugged named Michelangelo and Bernini as reference points.

The hotel's announcement made two promises that matter. The artist would be present to talk about his process, and more artists would follow.

Not a one-off

The same gallery lists a rolling residency at South Place Hotel in east London, with work by Zen Xander, Frank Canvas and Robi Walters. It records a three-month Zara Muse exhibition at a venue called Shanghai Noir in 2024. FAD Magazine reported a year-long display of her portraits at Fairmont Windsor Park.

Residency or decoration

What separates a residency from simply renting out pictures? Three things, we would suggest.

The first is change. If the work never rotates, it is décor. The second is the artist. A residency should mean the maker is named, credited and now and then in the room. The third is information. A guest should be able to find out what they are looking at without asking at reception.

What it means for artists

For an artist early in a career, a hotel offers something a small gallery cannot: hundreds of people a day with time on their hands. For the visitor it removes the awkwardness some feel about walking into a gallery at all.

The cost is control. A bar is noisy, the lighting is for atmosphere and nobody came for the art. Work shown there has to hold its own without help.

That is not a bad test. A picture that can stop someone on the way to breakfast is doing something right.

articles.title: Who Owns the Street? Public Art With and Without Permission
articles.summary: Some public art is commissioned. Some appears overnight. The interesting question is who gets to say yes.
articles.description: Public art is made with permission, without it, or somewhere in between. A feature on JR, Vhils, Konn Artiss and the question of who gets to decide.
articles.body:
A painting in a gallery has a simple chain of permission. The gallery owns the wall and chose the work. Step outside and it gets complicated at once. The wall has an owner. The street has a council. The neighbours have opinions. And the artist may not have asked any of them.

Three kinds of yes

It helps to separate three permissions that are often lumped together. There is the law, which decides whether marking a surface is a crime. There is the owner, who may or may not want a picture on their building. And there are the people who live with it every day.

These do not always agree. A legal mural can be resented by a whole street. An illegal one can be loved.

The case for not asking

The French artist JR has been frank about which permission matters to him. He told Elephant magazine that if the people in a place agree to a project, an official in an office should not be able to stop it, and that this is why much of his work is done illegally.

His project in Rio de Janeiro in 2008 shows the idea at its limit. To paste portraits of local women across a hillside favela, he did not go to the city. He went to the people who actually controlled the area, explained what he wanted to do and was allowed in.

The same artist, invited

Eight years later JR was back in Rio with full official blessing. For the 2016 Olympics he made The Giants, enormous images of athletes fitted to particular buildings. Same city, same artist, opposite arrangement.

That is the usual path. Vhils began as a teenage graffiti writer and now carves walls at festivals and on commission. Zen Xander is described as moving from the street to the gallery. Yesterday's trespass becomes today's invitation.

The uninvited guest

Then there is the artist who turns up at someone else's event. In October 2025, Konn Artiss left five blocks of ice outside the entrance to Frieze London, each holding a small figure of a famous artist. The published reports do not say whether anyone gave permission. The title, ANTI-FRIEZE, suggests what the answer would have been.

The work only makes sense in that spot. Move it to a gallery and it is a sculpture. Outside the fair, uninvited, it is a comment.

What permission changes

Permission is not neutral. A commissioned mural has been approved, which means someone decided it was safe. That is no insult to the work, but it shapes what can be said.

Work made without asking carries a risk that the commissioned kind does not, and viewers can feel it. The risk is also real for other people: the owner who has to clean a wall, the resident who never wanted a giant face outside the window.

A better question

So who owns the street? In law, the answer is clear enough. In practice, the street belongs to whoever uses it, and public art is one long argument about that.

The fairest test may be the one JR points to. Do the people who live with the work want it there? If they do, the paperwork tends to follow. If they do not, no amount of official approval will make it theirs.

articles.title: Vhils and the Art of Taking Away
articles.summary: Nearly every picture ever made was made by adding something to a surface. Vhils makes his by taking the surface away.
articles.description: Vhils carves portraits into city walls with chisels and jackhammers. A feature on the Portuguese artist and an art made by removing, not adding.
articles.alt: A large portrait of a man in a cap, made by chipping away the pale plaster of a tall brown city wall to show the darker layers beneath.
articles.credit: Joe Hatchiban, a wall portrait carved by Vhils (Alexandre Farto) in Berlin in 2011. Photographed in 2013. Photo: OTFW, Berlin, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
articles.body:
On the side of a worn building, a face several metres high looks out from the plaster. There is no paint on it. The light parts are where the old render still clings. The dark parts are where it has been cut back to brick.

This is the work of Alexandre Farto, who signs himself Vhils. He was born in 1987 and grew up on the edge of Lisbon, across the river from the city.

A boy with a spray can

He started writing graffiti at thirteen. His gallery tells how the walls around him were already crowded. After the revolution of 1974, Portuguese walls filled with political murals, and in the decades that followed those were buried under advertising, posters and more paint. A wall in his neighbourhood was a stack of years.

He later studied in London, at Byam Shaw and Central Saint Martins. The idea he arrived at was simple and odd. If the wall is made of layers, the picture is already in there. You only have to dig.

Scratching the Surface

He gave the method a plain name. By his own account, Scratching the Surface was first shown in Lisbon in 2007 and reached an international audience at the Cans Festival in London in 2008.

The process starts like a stencil. He marks out the portrait on the wall, deciding what will stay and what will go. Then the tools come out: chisels, hammers, drills, jackhammers. Reports of his work list acid and small explosive charges as well. What is left is a face in low relief, made of the wall's own history.

Whose faces

The people in the portraits are rarely famous. His gallery describes them as anonymous city dwellers, and notes that the walls he chooses are neglected or abandoned ones. A person nobody would paint, on a wall nobody would look at. The pairing is the point.

He has a phrase for what he does: an archaeology of the present.

Beyond the wall

The same thinking runs through his other work. In the studio he peels and cuts into thick pads of salvaged street posters. He has etched metal, carved wood and made pieces with controlled explosions. In each case the image comes from removing material.

The carved walls now appear in cities from Moscow to Sydney, and he has shown in galleries in London, Paris and Hong Kong.

Why it stays with you

Most public art puts something new in front of you. A Vhils portrait shows you what was already there, under the paint and the posters. It treats the city as a record that can be read.

It is also honest about time. The wall will keep crumbling. One day the face will go the way of everything else that was ever on that surface. Until then it looks back at the street that made it.

articles.title: Clarke Reynolds: Braille You Can See
articles.summary: Braille is written to be felt. Clarke Reynolds also wants it seen, in colour, at the size of a wall.
articles.description: Clarke Reynolds turns braille into colourful visual art meant to be touched. A note on how the work is made and who it is for.
articles.body:
Most art comes with a rule: do not touch. Clarke Reynolds makes work that asks for the opposite.

From one eye to none

Reynolds is based in Portsmouth. He has said he knew at six that he wanted to be an artist, after a visit to a local gallery. He was already blind in his right eye. In his early thirties he was diagnosed with retinitis pigmentosa, a condition that narrows the sight that remains.

Euronews reported that he had worked as a dental model maker and had to give the job up as his sight got worse. He kept making art and changed how he did it.

Dots as a language

Braille builds each letter from a cell of up to six raised dots. Reynolds takes that system and enlarges it. The dots become painted circles in strong colours, set out in the patterns of real letters and words. Sighted visitors see a field of colour. Anyone who reads braille can read what it says.

Arts Help quoted the text of one piece, in which he introduces himself as blind and as a visual artist who uses braille as his artistic language.

So the work operates twice. It is a picture and it is a sentence, and different people get to it by different routes.

Meant to be decoded

His first solo show, at the Yellow Edge Gallery in Gosport in 2021, was called Decoding Braille, Decoding Me. He described two visitors, one visually impaired and one sighted, spending about three hours racing each other to decode the works.

London followed in early 2023 with a solo exhibition at the Quantus Gallery, and in 2024 the Envision Arts Gallery in Wichita gave him his first solo show in the United States, with braille workshops in local schools alongside it.

Bigger dots

The scale keeps growing. In Tallahassee, Florida, in 2022, a local station reported dots three feet across, each the size of a pavement square, spelling the word love.

Who it is for

Reynolds also works under the name Mr Dot, a character he uses with children. The Big Issue reported that he is campaigning for braille to be taught in schools, as the system passes its two hundredth year.

The argument in the work is plain. A gallery that only lets you look has already decided who its visitors are. Change the material, and the audience changes with it.

articles.title: Paper, Paste and Scale: The Craft Behind JR's Street Portraits
articles.summary: A camera, a big printer, a bucket of paste and a wall. JR's method is simple enough that he has given it away.
articles.description: How JR makes his giant street portraits: black-and-white photographs, large-format paper and paste. A note on the craft and on the Inside Out Project.
articles.body:
The French artist JR, born in Paris in 1983, describes himself with a word of his own: photograffeur, part photographer and part graffiti writer. He takes portraits, prints them very large in black and white and pastes them onto buildings.

Three ingredients

The method has barely changed. First a photograph, usually a face, shot close. Then the print, on plain paper in strips large enough to cover a wall. Then the paste, brushed on by hand, often by teams of volunteers.

Each part is cheap. None of it is permanent. Rain and sun take the paper off within months. That is not a flaw in the work. A pasted portrait is closer to an event than to a monument.

Why so big

Scale does the arguing. A passport-sized face asks nothing of you. The same face six storeys high is hard to pass without wondering who it is.

His early series Portraits of a Generation, made between 2004 and 2006, showed young people from the housing estates around Paris in huge format. For Face 2 Face, the Brooklyn Museum records, he and his collaborators pasted large portraits side by side on both the Israeli and Palestinian sides of the separation wall.

Giving the method away

In 2011 JR won the TED Prize, worth 100,000 dollars, and used it to start the Inside Out Project. The idea was to hand his process to anyone who wanted it.

It works like this. A group takes its own portraits and sends them in. JR's studio prints them as posters and ships them back. The group pastes them up wherever it chooses. Phaidon's account adds that the team later built photobooth trucks that take a picture and print a large poster on the spot.

The numbers are large. By August 2022 there had been more than 2,300 group actions, with nearly half a million posters sent to 148 countries.

What the craft teaches

There is a lesson here for anyone who thinks ambitious art needs expensive materials. JR's kit could be bought on any high street. What makes the work is the decision about whose face goes where, and the labour of many people with brushes and ladders.

Paper, paste and scale. The rest is permission, or the lack of it.

articles.title: El Anatsui and the Second Life of Materials
articles.summary: Flatten a bottle cap, punch a hole in it, wire it to the next one. Repeat a few hundred thousand times.
articles.description: El Anatsui turns thousands of discarded bottle caps into vast hanging sculptures. A note on how they are made and why the material matters.
articles.alt: A weathered grey stone sculpture of a crouching, rounded figure whose large hands cover its face, set on paving in front of a yellow concrete building.
articles.credit: Ambivalent Hold, from a design by El Anatsui, made by the SKEP art collective for the Physical Sciences building at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka. Photographed in 2024. Photo: Mercyjamb123, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
articles.body:
From a distance, an El Anatsui hanging looks like cloth of gold. It folds and ripples and catches the light. Walk up to it and you find it is made of rubbish: the aluminium caps and collars from liquor bottles, each one flattened and wired to its neighbours.

A bag by the road

Anatsui was born in Anyako, Ghana, in 1944, and has worked for decades in Nigeria, with a studio also in Tema, Ghana. The story of the bottle caps is often told. In 1998, walking near Nsukka in Nigeria, he noticed a bag of them by the roadside and took it back to the studio.

He began to experiment: folding the caps, slicing them into rounds, opening out the sides. With assistants he found a method that worked. The metal is pierced in several places and the pieces are linked with copper wire.

Many hands

The scale needs a workshop. Sculpture magazine described teams of assistants, recruited near his studios, who clip, flatten and link the caps into sheets. Those sheets are modules. Ocula's account of his process has Anatsui stepping in at the end to arrange them into the final composition.

He has said that the colours of the caps, the yellows, blacks and reds, led him to think like a painter as well as a sculptor.

Nothing is fixed

Because the sheets are flexible, the works have no single correct shape. They can be draped, bunched or stretched, and they are hung differently each time they are shown. The people installing them make real decisions. That is unusual for sculpture, and deliberate.

The Turbine Hall

The largest test came in London. For Tate Modern's Hyundai Commission, Anatsui made Behind the Red Moon, shown in the Turbine Hall from 10 October 2023 to 14 April 2024. It came in three parts: The Red Moon, The World and The Wall.

Tate's guide describes thousands of bottle tops and metal fragments crumpled, crushed and joined by hand. The first hanging, in red, formed the outline of a moon in eclipse and billowed like a sail.

Why bottle caps

The material is not neutral. Liquor was one of the goods traded along the routes that carried enslaved people across the Atlantic, and Tate's guide ties the work to those histories of power and survival. The caps are cheap, local and plentiful. They also carry a past.

That is the second life of the title. The object is saved from the roadside, and its history comes with it.

articles.title: Painting Without a Brush: Knives, Fingers and Chisels
articles.summary: A palette knife, a fingertip, a chisel. Three artists who gave up the brush, and what each one got in return.
articles.description: Three artists who put the brush down: Zara Muse with a palette knife, Amoako Boafo with his fingers and Vhils with a chisel. A note on tools and what they change.
articles.body:
The brush is such an ordinary part of painting that we rarely ask what it does. It holds paint, it draws a line, it softens an edge. It also puts fifteen centimetres of wood between the artist and the picture. Some artists decide they want that distance gone.

The knife

Zara Muse told Art Plugged that she works only with a palette knife and a spatula. A knife cannot draw a thin line or blend gently. It lays paint down in flat pieces with clear edges. A face built this way is made of planes, and the paint stands proud of the canvas. The limit is the point. It forces decisions.

The finger

Amoako Boafo went further and removed the tool altogether. According to Colección SOLO, he began painting with his fingers in 2017. He does not do it everywhere. Accounts of his method note that the skin of his sitters is finger-painted in oil, while clothes and backgrounds are often handled with brushes and paper transfer.

So in a Boafo portrait you can see exactly where the hand has been. The body is alive with swirls. Everything around it is still.

The chisel

The Portuguese artist Vhils, born Alexandre Farto in 1987, does not add anything at all. He takes away. Using chisels, mallets, picks and jackhammers, he cuts into the plaster of old walls until a portrait appears in the layers underneath.

He calls the approach Scratching the Surface. His own biography dates its first public showing to Lisbon in 2007 and its international debut to the Cans Festival in London in 2008. The faces are usually of ordinary, unnamed people, and the walls are ones a city has neglected.

His gallery traces the idea to the walls he grew up with outside Lisbon, thick with decades of posters and paint. To carve into them is to read the history of the place.

What the tool decides

Put the three side by side and a pattern shows. Each tool leaves a different kind of evidence. The knife leaves an edge. The finger leaves a touch. The chisel leaves a wound that becomes a face.

None of this makes the brush wrong. But a change of tool is never only technical. It changes how close the artist stands, how fast they can work and what kind of mistake is possible. The picture you end up looking at is, in part, a record of that choice.

articles.title: Njideka Akunyili Crosby: Two Homes in One Picture
articles.summary: From across the room it is a quiet domestic scene. Up close, the walls and floors turn out to be made of hundreds of photographs.
articles.description: Njideka Akunyili Crosby layers paint, collage and photo transfer to picture a life between Nigeria and the United States. A reported profile.
articles.alt: Njideka Akunyili Crosby, with her hair pulled back, speaking in a plain white room during a filmed interview.
articles.credit: Njideka Akunyili Crosby interviewed by the Bronx Museum Teen Council, November 2014. A still from their film. Photo: Bronx Museum Teen Council, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
articles.body:
A couple at a table. A woman on a sofa. A room with a patterned floor. Njideka Akunyili Crosby paints ordinary moments at home. Then you step closer and the surfaces dissolve into images: faces, magazine pages, family snapshots, printed into the picture itself.

Enugu to Los Angeles

She was born in Enugu, Nigeria, in 1983, and moved to the United States at sixteen to continue her education. She studied at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts and at Yale, and now lives and works in Los Angeles.

How the pictures are built

Her works combine acrylic paint, charcoal, coloured pencil, fabric, collage and photo transfer. The transfers are made with acetone, which lifts a printed image and sets it down on the paper, slightly softened.

The source material is personal. She uses photographs she has taken in Nigeria, pictures from family albums and pages from popular Nigerian magazines. Laid side by side, they become wallpaper, clothing and floors inside the painted room.

Two worlds, one room

The Carnegie Corporation, which named her among its Great Immigrants in 2020, describes work that ranges from the legacy of colonialism in Africa to the experience of being an immigrant in America. What is striking is how gently it is done. Nothing is announced. A Nigerian pop star sits in the pattern of a dress. A family portrait is half hidden in the floor.

The effect is close to how memory works. The present scene is in front of you, and the past is in everything around it.

Recognition

In 2017 she received a MacArthur Fellowship, often called the genius grant. In 2018 the National Portrait Gallery in London showed her series The Beautyful Ones. She is represented by Victoria Miro and David Zwirner.

Why it matters

Many artists have pictured life between two countries as a kind of split. Akunyili Crosby pictures it as a layering. Both homes are present at once, in the same room, on the same sheet of paper. That is a more accurate account of how a great many people now live.

articles.title: Amoako Boafo and the Portrait Painted by Hand
articles.summary: He paints faces and hands with his own fingers. You can see the touch in every one of them.
articles.description: Amoako Boafo paints the skin of his sitters with his fingers. A reported profile of the Ghanaian artist, from Accra to Vienna and back.
articles.alt: Amoako Boafo in a white T-shirt, sitting on the edge of a white table in his studio, with large unfinished portraits of figures on pink and pale blue grounds on the walls behind him.
articles.credit: Amoako Boafo in his studio, July 2020. Photo: Francis Kokoroko, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
articles.body:
Look closely at the skin in an Amoako Boafo portrait. It is made of swirls and ridges of oil paint, blues and browns pushed around by a fingertip. The clothes and the background are flat and calm. All the movement is in the body.

Accra to Vienna

Boafo was born in Accra, Ghana, on 10 May 1984. He studied at the Ghanatta College of Art and Design there, and later at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna. Artnet records that he moved to Vienna in 2014 and began a series of portraits of Black people he met in the city.

Vienna gave him two things. One was the example of Egon Schiele and the painters of the Vienna Secession, with their twisting, expressive figures. The other, by several accounts, was the experience of seeing how rarely Black subjects appeared on the walls around him.

The fingers

According to Colección SOLO, it was in 2017 that he decided to start painting with his fingers. The technique is selective. One detailed account notes that he finger-paints exposed skin in oil and uses brushes and paper transfer for much of the clothing, objects and backgrounds.

The effect is that touch itself becomes part of the meaning. These are portraits of friends, family and people he admires, and the paint on their faces has been laid there by hand.

A fast rise

The art market noticed quickly. Ocula reports that in 2020 his painting The Lemon Bathing Suit, made the year before, sold at auction for £675,000. The same year he worked with Dior on a fashion collection.

Museums followed. Soul of Black Folks opened at the Museum of the African Diaspora in San Francisco in 2021 and travelled to the Denver Art Museum in 2023. In 2024 the Belvedere in Vienna showed more than fifty works under the title Proper Love, hanging some beside Schiele and Klimt.

Home again

It would be easy to tell this as a story about prices. A better one is about place. Recent profiles give Accra as the centre of his studio and of the cultural projects he supports, with Vienna still part of the picture. The painter who left to study has gone back to build something.

articles.title: Amanza Smith Starts Again on Canvas
articles.summary: Television audiences know the name already. The paintings ask to be looked at without it.
articles.description: Amanza Smith, known from television, made her debut as a painter at MASH Gallery in Los Angeles. A reported profile of her mixed media work.
articles.body:
Amanza Smith came to painting with a public profile. She is known to television viewers from the property series Selling Sunset, and her gallery describes her simply as multifaceted. The question any such artist faces is whether the work holds up once the name is covered.

A debut in Los Angeles

She made her debut as an exhibiting artist at MASH Gallery in Los Angeles. The gallery's account notes that she is from Indiana and calls her no stranger to reinvention.

What the paintings are made of

The work is mixed media on canvas, often large. In The Groove, from 2024, measures 130 centimetres square and, according to the gallery's notes, brings collage into the paint, including images of Frida Kahlo. City Zen, from the same year, is larger still and is described as graffiti lifted into fine art, a reflection on life in a big city.

More recent pieces turn to machines. Gallery notes for works such as Circuit Riot describe robotic forms, circuitry and glitch-like marks set against loose, gestural paint.

Words in the paint

Text appears too. Of the painting To The Bone, the gallery reports that she wrote the word love across the surface several times, as a deliberate act of encouragement.

Some viewers will find that too direct. But it is consistent. These are open-hearted pictures, more interested in energy than in irony.

To Europe

In April 2025 her work crossed the Atlantic. Grove Gallery opened a space in Palma with a first exhibition, Beyond The Surface, showing her alongside Zara Muse and Silent Mike.

A fair test

Fame gets an artist through the door quickly, and it also means many people decide what they think before they look. The fair test is the ordinary one. Stand in front of the canvas. See whether the colour, the layering and the marks keep your attention once you stop thinking about who made them.

articles.title: Robi Walters: Petals Cut from Broken Records
articles.summary: He cuts petals from broken vinyl and old packaging, and arranges them into flowers that seem to burst off the wall.
articles.description: Robi Walters builds lotus-like collages from broken vinyl records and discarded packaging. A reported profile of his practice, materials and daily routine.
articles.body:
Robi Walters was born in London in 1973 and still works there. His material is what other people throw away.

Rubbish, rearranged

The collages are made from discarded flyers, cardboard, household packaging and broken vinyl records. He cuts these into petal shapes, hundreds of them, and layers them outward from a centre. The Week described the effect as an explosive three-dimensional collage of colour, like fireworks or bursts of lotus flowers.

The lotus is not an accident. House Collective traced the work to sacred geometry and to the Buddhist symbol of the thousand-petal lotus, and to the calm Walters looks for in meditation.

A day with two ends

His routine has a shape. An artist profile published in 2017 notes that he meditates every morning and ends each day by making a painting, a kind of diary in paint. Cent Magazine reported where the habit came from: the Turner Prize winner Chris Ofili advised him to paint every day, and he took the advice literally.

So there are two bodies of work running side by side. The slow, exact collages, and the quick daily paintings that keep the hand moving.

Where it comes from

Walters has spoken openly about a difficult childhood. The Week reported that he was fostered and spent time in and out of children's homes. He told one interviewer that he cannot separate his early life from the work, and gave the recycled material as the example. Cent Magazine noted that he is now close to both his mother and his foster family.

House Collective describes him as self-taught. In that light the choice of material reads less like a style and more like a statement: nothing is beyond being made into something.

Recognition

The Week reported that at forty-four he opened a gallery of his own in Soho. More recently, Grove Gallery lists his work in its residency at South Place Hotel in east London.

Stand in front of one of the collages and you can still read fragments of the old life of the material: a groove, a scrap of lettering, the edge of a label. That is the point. The record is broken. It has become something else.

articles.title: Frank Canvas and the One-Line Joke
articles.summary: Some pictures need a wall text. A Frank Canvas needs a title of three words or fewer.
articles.description: Frank Canvas makes satirical limited edition prints with one-line titles. A short reported profile, drawn from his gallery's published material.
articles.body:
A note on sources first. Almost everything published about Frank Canvas comes from Grove Gallery, which represents and sells his work. We have found no independent interview or review. So this is a short profile, and it leans on the gallery's own description.

What the gallery says

Grove Gallery calls him an emerging artist who blends humour, satire and social commentary. Elsewhere it describes a bold, tongue-in-cheek approach to contemporary culture, with work meant to challenge, entertain and start conversations.

The titles do the talking

The clearest evidence is the list of titles. My Favourite Park. Choose Your Reality. Shopaholic. Karma. Coffee. Better Days. I Like. Each reads like the caption to a cartoon, or a message typed with one thumb. They point at the small rituals of modern life: shopping, caffeine, self-improvement, the phone.

This is satire at the scale of the everyday. The targets are not politicians or institutions. They are habits most of us recognise in ourselves.

Made to be owned

The format matters as much as the joke. The gallery lists the works as signed limited editions, typically in runs of 125, as prints and on canvas in sizes from A3 to A0. That is a deliberate choice. It keeps prices within reach of someone buying art for the first time, and it means the same image hangs in many homes.

There is a long line of artists who have worked this way, from the pop artists of the 1960s to the street artists whose prints sell out online in minutes. The edition is the artwork's natural form, not a souvenir of some larger original.

On the wall

Grove Gallery records his work in its rolling residency at South Place Hotel in east London, shown with Zen Xander and Robi Walters. A hotel suits this kind of picture. It is seen in passing, and it has a few seconds to make a stranger smile.

We would like to know more: where he trained, how the images are made, what he reads. When we can report that first-hand, we will.

articles.title: Zen Xander: One Name, Many Hands
articles.summary: A lion in a virtual reality headset eating salad. The joke lands at once. The harder question is who made it.
articles.description: Zen Xander is described as an anonymous street artist and, on the artist's own site, as a collective. A reported profile of the satirical stencil work.
articles.body:
Most artist profiles begin with a person. This one cannot, because the accounts of who Zen Xander is do not agree.

Two versions

When Grove Gallery in Fitzrovia opened Society Falling in June 2024, Art Plugged introduced Zen Xander as an anonymous street artist known for a satirical approach to fine art, moving from the street into the gallery. Artsy lists the show as a first solo exhibition, running from 26 June to 31 July 2024.

The artist's own website tells it differently. It says Zen Xander is not a single artist but a small group of painters, illustrators, designers and writers who share one aim: to make art that is warm, funny and easy to recognise yourself in.

We cannot settle which account is the fuller one, and we will not guess. It is worth noticing that both can be true of a name. A signature can belong to a studio as easily as to a hand.

The work

What is not in doubt is what the pictures look like. Animals are placed in human situations and left to carry the argument. Art Plugged described VR Vegan, in which a lion wears a virtual reality headset while eating a bowl of salad, as a jab at the gap between real and virtual life and at the contradictions of modern diets.

The method comes from the street. Artsy records the works in Society Falling, among them Nut Hacker, Drone Cat and Always a Cheetah, as hand-cut stencil and spray paint on plywood, each roughly a metre across.

Why animals

Satire needs a little distance. Put a person in the picture and the viewer starts asking who it is meant to be. Put a cheetah or a cat there and everyone is free to see themselves. It is an old trick, as old as fables, and it suits an artist, or a group of artists, who would rather not be the story.

Out of the gallery

The work has not stayed in Fitzrovia. Grove Gallery's own record of its exhibitions lists Zen Xander pieces at South Place Hotel in east London, alongside Frank Canvas and Robi Walters, and a continuation of Society Falling at a Dorsett hotel in London.

An anonymous name, a recognisable style and a joke that reads in two seconds. Whoever holds the spray can, the formula is clear.

articles.title: Portraiture, Celebrity and Contemporary Cultural Memory
articles.summary: A portrait of a famous face is never only a likeness. It is a bid for how that person will be remembered.
articles.description: How contemporary portraiture turns public figures into cultural icons, from Warhol's Marilyn to Zara Muse's Malala and Konn Artiss's melting effigies.
articles.body:
In 1962, within weeks of Marilyn Monroe's death, Andy Warhol made the Marilyn Diptych. Fifty repeated faces, half in bright colour and half fading to grey. More than sixty years on, it is hard to picture Monroe without picturing Warhol's version of her.

That is the power of the celebrity portrait. It does not just record fame. It fixes a particular image of it in the shared memory.

Who gets painted now

For most of history the answer was simple: whoever could pay. Kings, merchants, their families. The portrait was proof of standing. Today artists more often choose their own subjects, and the choice is itself a statement about who deserves a place on the wall.

Zara Muse chose Malala Yousafzai. She told Art Plugged the subject stood for resilience, bravery and strength. The portrait sold at Bonhams in London in April 2025 for £51,200 including premium. Set aside the price and look at the decision. A painter known for portraits of women picked a living campaigner for girls' education and gave her the full weight of thick paint and saturated colour. That is an argument about who our icons should be.

When the famous are artists

Konn Artiss turned the same lens on the art world. For ANTI-FRIEZE in October 2025, the anonymous artist froze small effigies of Damien Hirst, Andy Warhol, Tracey Emin, Jeff Koons and KAWS in blocks of ice outside Frieze London and let them melt.

Art Plugged read the work as a comment on artistic immortality. It is also, in its odd way, a group portrait. These five are among the few artists famous enough to be recognised as dolls. The piece asks how long that kind of fame lasts once the conditions around it change.

Memory is a choice

Put the two beside each other and a pattern shows. One artist builds a face up in paint so that it will last. The other builds faces in ice so that they will not. Both are working on the same material, which is public memory.

A portrait of a living person is always a little early. The story is not finished and the painter is guessing at the ending. That is what makes the form risky, and why it still matters. When you next stand in front of a famous face in paint, ask who chose it, and what they are hoping you will remember.

articles.title: When Art Enters the World of Luxury Hospitality
articles.summary: Paintings are leaving the white room for the hotel bar. It is worth asking what they gain there, and what they give up.
articles.description: What happens when contemporary art moves into luxury hotels and restaurants, with Zara Muse at Fairmont Windsor Park as a case study in cultural partnerships.
articles.body:
A gallery asks for a certain kind of attention. You go on purpose, you stand, you look, you leave. A hotel asks for nothing. People sit for an hour with a drink and the painting is simply there, at the edge of the conversation.

A case in Windsor

In November 2024, FAD Magazine reported on a year-long partnership between Grove Gallery and the Fairmont Windsor Park hotel. Fourteen works from a new collection by Zara Muse were hung in the hotel's Bar 1215 and in its fine dining restaurant.

The launch was tied to a second partnership. Astrea London, which makes lab-grown diamonds, opened a boutique in the hotel, and Muse made a centrepiece portrait called Revolution that incorporates a 14.9 carat diamond.

It is not a one-off. Luxury News Online reported in March 2025 that her work also hangs in Kanishka, a restaurant in Mayfair, and that she had expanded into Dubai. Art Plugged described her paintings in hotel lobbies and private homes across Europe and the Middle East.

What the art gains

The first gain is time. A guest may spend longer near a painting in a bar than most visitors spend in front of anything in a museum. The second is audience. Many people who would never walk into a commercial gallery will happily spend an evening in a hotel.

FAD quoted the gallery's own view: that art should be accessible and part of everyday life, and that these rooms let it become part of the surroundings instead of a static display.

What it risks

The risk is the same thing seen from the other side. Art that becomes part of the surroundings can become furniture. Hotels choose work that suits a mood, and difficult or uncomfortable pictures rarely make the cut. A painting set beside a diamond is also, plainly, being asked to do a job for a brand.

Questions for the visitor

None of that is a reason to look away. It is a reason to look properly. Next time you find a painting in a hotel, ask three things. Is the artist named? Is there anything to tell you about the work? Could you see it without booking a table? The answers say a good deal about whether the art is a guest in the room or just part of the décor.

articles.title: Konn Artiss and the Relationship Between Object and Spectacle
articles.summary: A block of ice, a parody newspaper, a mannequin on a canal. Konn Artiss makes objects that are built to disappear, and events that are built to stay.
articles.description: Konn Artiss makes objects designed to vanish: melting ice, a parody newspaper, a floating mannequin. A reported essay on public interventions and spectacle.
articles.body:
On the morning visitors arrived at Frieze London in October 2025, five large blocks of ice were standing outside the main entrance. Art Plugged reported that each weighed 40 stone and each held a miniature effigy of a famous name: Damien Hirst, Andy Warhol, Tracey Emin, Jeff Koons and KAWS.

The work was called ANTI-FRIEZE. Then it melted. By the account in Art Plugged, what remained was puddles, bananas and a crowd caught between curiosity and discomfort.

An artist nobody has met

Konn Artiss is anonymous. The name first drew wide attention in June 2025. FAD Magazine reported a stunt in Washington DC built around The Washington Ghost, a parody newspaper aimed at Jeff Bezos shortly before his wedding in Venice. FAD noted that the name Konn Artiss had surfaced on social media with the sign-off "Trust Me".

The action then moved to Venice itself. GB News reported mannequins of Bezos and his fiancée floating along the Grand Canal in a gondola, and said more than 10,000 copies of the newspaper had been handed out.

The object

Look at what these works are made of. Frozen water. Newsprint. Shop mannequins. Fruit. None of it is meant to last, and none of it can be hung on a wall and sold in the usual way. The ice is the clearest case. It is a sculpture with a clock inside it.

The bananas are harder to read. It is difficult not to think of Maurizio Cattelan, who taped one to a wall at an art fair in 2019 and watched it become one of the most discussed artworks of the decade. That reading is ours, not the artist's.

The spectacle

If the object vanishes, where is the artwork? Mostly in what happens around it: the people who stop, the photographs they take, the reports that follow. Art Plugged read ANTI-FRIEZE as a comment on value, hype and decay, and on an art market that prizes permanence. The melting made that argument without a word of wall text.

This is the tension the work lives on. It mocks spectacle and depends on it completely. An intervention that nobody photographs has, in practical terms, not happened.

What is left

What stays behind is the record and the question. With an anonymous artist there is no biography to lean on, and with a melted sculpture there is no object to revisit. We are left to decide whether the event said something true. In October 2025, outside the tent where art is bought and sold, a lot of people stopped to watch famous names drip away. That is worth reporting.

articles.title: The Role of Personal Experience in Artistic Practice
articles.summary: A life does not explain a painting. But it often explains why the painting exists at all.
articles.description: How lived experience shapes artistic practice, from Zara Muse's return to painting to artists who withhold their biography altogether.
articles.body:
Ask an artist where the work comes from and the first answer is usually about materials or method. The second answer, if you wait for it, is usually about something that happened to them.

One account

Zara Muse has been open about hers. In an interview with Art Plugged in April 2025 she described caring for her mother through cancer, and her mother's death in February 2019. She said the loss changed her and made her more determined. She began painting again during the lockdown of 2020.

She has also spoken about what she left behind. Before painting she worked in finance and trading. She told the same interviewer that the old career does not feed directly into the pictures, but that leaving it gave her room to find herself. The portraits that followed are of women, and she describes them as a tribute to resilience.

None of this tells you whether a given portrait is good. What it tells you is what the artist was looking for when she picked up the knife.

A long tradition

She is in old company. Frida Kahlo began painting in earnest while confined to bed after a bus accident in 1925, and her own body remained her subject for the rest of her life. Louise Bourgeois returned to her childhood again and again across a career that lasted into her nineties. Tracey Emin showed her own unmade bed in 1998 and made the private life of the artist a public question.

The risk

There is a danger in all this. A moving story can be used to sell a weak picture, and a strong picture can be flattened into an illustration of its maker's biography. Viewers are right to be wary when the story arrives before the work does.

The opposite choice

Some artists refuse the bargain entirely. Konn Artiss, whose public interventions we report on in this issue, works anonymously. There is no childhood, no studio portrait and no origin story on offer. The work has to stand on what it does in the street.

Both approaches are honest in their way. One says: this is where it came from. The other says: that is none of your business, look at the thing. As readers and viewers, our job is the same in each case. Look first. Then, if the artist has offered it, listen to the story and see whether the work can carry it.
